Science.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
Science.summary: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

Science.title: Disasters and debt. Escaping the 'climate-debt doom loop'
Science.summary: It took around 480,000 trucks to haul away 4.8 million metric tons (5.3 million tons) of rubble across western Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa tore through the Caribbean in 2025, United Nations satellites showed.

Science.title: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests
Science.summary: An alternative model in which the universe is 26.7 billion years old and needs neither dark matter nor dark energy has held up against several major cosmology tests, according to a new University of Ottawa study. The research, titled "A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology," is published in the journal Universe.

Science.title: AI won't ever make a historically accurate film—but it could help archaeology create better stories
Science.summary: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer's "Odyssey" by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticized for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story "historically accurate and true to the art of Homer" at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.

Science.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

Science.title: Tectonic forces near Japan helped fuel the formation of the Grand Canyon
Science.summary: A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

Science.title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it's a cause for joy
Science.summary: It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound (6,804-kilogram) baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn't be happier.

Science.title: Student finds proof of rare wild cat in northern New Mexico
Science.summary: Armed with dozens of motion-sensing cameras, William Grooms spent this past summer documenting wildlife across Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. It was his first field season collecting photos for a two-year study to understand how forest structure influences biodiversity in the Southern Rocky Mountains.

Science.title: Pakistani astronaut to board Shenzhou 24 and become the first foreigner on China's space station
Science.summary: A Pakistani astronaut will join the crew of China's Shenzhou 24 spacecraft on a mission that would make him the first foreign national to board Beijing's space station, state media reported Saturday.

Science.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
Science.summary: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible. The study, published in Science, provides an important foundation for future quantum simulations of nuclear physics and materials science.

Science.title: New ‘high safety’ chemicals in plastic food packaging linked to lower birth weight, study finds
Science.summary: Dinch, an allegedly ‘safe’ alternative, used in the EU and US also found to cause fetal development complications Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found. As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety” , nontoxic alternative. Science.title: How a metabolite protects the enzyme that consumes it
Science.summary: Metabolites are consumed by enzymes to produce other vital molecules as well as to control metabolite levels. But how do cells avoid consuming too much? Researchers from the MPI of Biochemistry, with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and the de Duve Institute in Brussels, have deciphered such molecular regulation in tryptophan metabolism. The essential amino acid tryptophan binds to a second site on the enzyme TDO2, distinct from where it is consumed. This sequesters a region needed by two effectors, the kinase CK2 and the ubiquitin ligase CUL1–β-TrCP, which act sequentially to signal TDO2

Science.title: MTG-I2 satellite delivers remarkable first images, capturing a weather view of Europe every 2.5 minutes
Science.summary: Europe's meteorological satellite agency, EUMETSAT, has released the first image from the Flexible Combined Imager (FCI) on board Meteosat Third Generation Imager 2 (MTG-I2), just over two months after the satellite's launch on Aug. 27, 2026. The satellite will provide forecasters with high-resolution observations of Europe every 2.5 minutes. This unprecedented frequency will help forecasters monitor fast-developing weather hazards more closely and support earlier, more precise warnings.

Science.title: SpaceX launches mystery mission for US Space Force in gorgeous sunset liftoff from California (video, photos)
Science.summary: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Nov. 6). It was the company's 125th liftoff of 2026.

Science.title: Future warming events will outdo the extreme heat waves of the recent past, new study finds
Science.summary: The extreme heat waves we have seen over the last few years may only serve as a preview of what is to come as a result of climate change. A new study led by researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner from Freie Universität Berlin, published in Nature Communications, finds that future heat waves could last longer, impact larger areas, and be much more severe.

Science.title: Light-powered method resurrects 'dead-end' compounds for drug discovery
Science.summary: Throughout the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never go on to become medicines. A Florida State University researcher is part of a team that has discovered a new way to give some of these "dead ends" a second chance at becoming the foundation for tomorrow's blockbuster drugs.

Science.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
Science.summary: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight. Science.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
Science.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

Science.title: European forests need to solve two crises—but not necessarily in one place
Science.summary: Forest areas can act both as carbon sinks and as vital habitats for thousands of species—but not necessarily at the same time. This has important implications for how Europe should manage its forests, says a University of Copenhagen researcher.

Science.title: Earth's gravity may have kept the early moon's volcanic heart beating
Science.summary: We typically think of the moon as a static, floating object that has remained the same for basically its entire lifetime, with an occasional asteroid impact serving as an exception. That understanding is grounded in physics—the moon should have cooled rapidly after forming when a huge protoplanet hit the early Earth around 4.5 billion years ago. But some lunar material returned from the Chang'e-5 mission was notably formed only around 2 billion years ago, yet appeared to be volcanic in origin.

Science.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
Science.summary: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

Science.title: The hidden ways insects support animal life—from habitat to health—go way beyond being food
Science.summary: There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth, and they play highly diverse roles in sustaining the natural world. Insects provide many well-known benefits—what scientists often call "ecosystem services." For example, you can thank a bee or a hoverfly for pollinating wildflowers and agricultural crops, or credit dung beetles for decomposing manure and other waste materials.

Science.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
Science.summary: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.

Science.title: Heavy rain can more than double glacier speeds in Alaska
Science.summary: Glaciers are often thought of as unyielding blocks of ice that slowly carve out the landscape as they move downhill by gravity. But sometimes their slow crawl becomes a surge that sees them move orders of magnitude faster than their usual speed.

Science.title: AST SpaceMobile announces new 'Blacklift' rocket, targets 2028 launch debut
Science.summary: AST SpaceMobile plans to launch its broadband satellites on a new rocket called Blacklift, which it will build in house and plans to start flying in 2028.

Science.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission
Science.summary: NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan.

Science.title: Scientists discover new jellyfish species in waters off Alicante in Spain
Science.summary: The Mediterranean Sea still holds species unknown to science. One of them is Copula lucentia, a tiny jellyfish measuring just a few millimeters. Discovered off El Campello, in Alicante, it was formally described in 2024 by a research team at the University of Alicante (UA) Marine Laboratory in Dénia, which forms part of the university's Ramón Margalef Multidisciplinary Institute for Environmental Research.

Science.title: The Maya used so much red paint that they poisoned their water with mercury, mud sediments reveal
Science.summary: Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

Science.title: Personalized savings reminders can help boost retirement savings
Science.summary: Private retirement savings are an increasingly important topic in public debate. One popular idea is to phrase savings reminders in one of two ways: either you emphasize what someone stands to lose if they don't save, or you emphasize what they stand to gain if they do. To date, research into which of the two reminder messages is more effective in terms of influencing people's efforts to save has produced conflicting results.

Science.title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
Science.summary: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

Science.title: High-precision timeline helps clarify an ancient magma surge in the North Cascades
Science.summary: Where oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, belts of volcanoes known as continental arcs can form. Located around the world, these arcs may undergo episodic magma flare-ups—dramatic surges in the flow of magma into the continental crust at rates up to 20 times higher than normal. However, what triggers these extreme surges, which last tens of millions of years, can be unclear.

Science.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
Science.summary: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.

Science.summary: Hear Neil Armstrong's son and granddaughter sing a moving tribute to the legendary Apollo 11 astronaut

Science.title: 'Life is too brief to leave this planet': Live Science readers share whether they'd go to Mars, despite health risks
Science.summary: Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

Science.title: New method measures microplastics in the air using an uncrewed aerial system
Science.summary: Microplastics have been found in our bodies and the food we eat—and even in remote environments around the world, including seawater and ice in the Arctic. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how they move through the atmosphere. New CIRES-led research, which demonstrates a new method for sampling microplastics in the atmosphere using an uncrewed aerial system (UAS), aims to change that. The findings are published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Science.title: Polar vortex faltering weeks earlier than ever recorded
Science.summary: Meteorologists said Friday they were observing an unprecedented early disruption of the polar vortex, raising the risk of cold snaps across the Northern Hemisphere, though there remains significant uncertainty.

Science.title: Untangling the patterns of the cosmic microwave background to better understand the early universe
Science.summary: A figure in red trudges across a blanket of white. Snow squeaks under the scientist's feet, too dry to be slick or soft. Only a line of flags and a few large buildings—the scientist's destination—break up the landscape. The sun hovers on the horizon, never quite setting against a blue sky devoid of clouds.

Science.title: Why treating soil acidity crop by crop is no longer enough for prairie farmers
Science.summary: To protect their future harvests, Western Canadian farmers need to manage soil acidity across their entire multiyear rotation rather than crop by crop, long-term research from the University of Alberta suggests.

Science.title: Women often get cold more easily than men — a mouse study offers hints why
Science.summary: A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

Science.title: The introduction of a medieval public health system exposed the population to roundworm
Science.summary: Medieval health and sanitation efforts involved deliberate interventions; however, some of these measures had the opposite effect, leading to an increased spread of disease in Trondheim.

Science.title: Two paths, one flux: Trapped ions simulate Aharonov–Bohm interference in a lattice gauge theory
Science.summary: In a new Nature Physics study, researchers demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer.

Science.title: Different text genres help doctoral students adapt their writing to reach new readers
Science.summary: An academic abstract, a blog post and a public outreach article all place different demands on the writer. Readers' prior knowledge varies, as does the purpose of the text and what needs explaining. Mastering one kind of text therefore does not automatically mean being able to write another.

Science.title: The wasps that horrified Darwin reveal evolution's one-way streets
Science.summary: Few insects have a more gruesome lifestyle than Darwin wasps. Rather than simply hunting other animals, these parasitic wasps lay their eggs on or inside living hosts, including caterpillars, beetles and spiders. Their larvae then feed on their hosts, gradually consuming them and eventually killing them.

Science.title: Spot a baby bird on the ground? Don't be tempted to bird‑nap it
Science.summary: Spring is the season of blooming flowers and buzzing bees.

Science.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
Science.summary: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make metasurfaces strongly absorb UV light.

Science.title: Star Wars is experiencing a golden age of video games
Science.summary: The movies might be struggling to recapture the magic, but Star Wars video games are strong with the Force.

Science.title: Why do most cats hate it when you touch their belly, feet or tail?
Science.summary: The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

Science.title: I almost died from flu. My life didn't go back to normal after.
Science.summary: Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

Science.title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
Science.summary: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.

Science.title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer
Science.summary: For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.
